newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Arafat calls conference, Israel rejects pressure.
newsitem.headline: Arafat calls conference, Israel rejects pressure.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat sought on Tuesday to draw the United States deeper into salvaging Middle East peace talks that have foundered on Israeli settlement plans in the West Bank.

The PLO chairman invited U.S., European and Arab envoys to a meeting on Saturday to discuss a crisis brewing since Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu approved plans to build Jewish housing between Arab East Jerusalem and Bethlehem.

The United States, Israel's closest ally, said it would attend the meeting while Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy warned that PLO efforts to bring international pressure on the Jewish state could freeze peace moves.

"Any appeal which could bring about international involvement could -- and I am warning that such a danger exists even if Israel does not want it to come about -- bring about a freeze in the political process," Levy told reporters in a hastily convened news conference.
Jordan's King Hussein, the Arab leader closest to Netanyahu, accused the Israeli prime minister of turning Middle East peace into a "distant elusive mirage" with his policies.
"My distress is genuine and deep over the accumulating tragic actions which you have initiated," King Hussein told Netanyahu in a letter dated March 9 and made available to Reuters in Amman.
"I could remain aloof if the very lives of all Arabs and Israelis and their future were not fast sliding towards an abyss of bloodshed, brought about by fear and despair," the king said.

Arafat, feeling the frustration of the Palestinian street and of his own PLO colleagues, has tried to rally support at the United Nations and among Western and Moslem countries for halting the settlement.
The crisis deepened last Friday when Israel disclosed the depth of the first of three West Bank pullbacks. It offered the Palestinians about a third of what they wanted.
U.S. State Department Spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Tuesday that Washington understood "the frustration of the Palestinian leadership" and Arafat's initiative was natural.

"We certainly, if an invitation is formally issued to the United States, will be there," Burns told reporters. "Chairman Arafat obviously feels the need to talk to friendly countries around the world, and that's appropriate."

Underscoring tensions, an Israeli soldier guarding a West Bank Jewish settlement near Hebron was stabbed 20 times and wounded seriously in an apparent Palestinian guerrilla attack, military sources said on Tuesday. The two attackers fled with his gun.

Levy said Arafat's move was an attempt to wring greater territorial concessions from Israel in the next two West Bank redeployments, which must be completed by mid-1998 under peace deals with the PLO.
"No one should be enticed into thinking that by doing so they will be able to pressure Israel to act against its will and interests," said Levy.
Saeb Erekat, a Palestinian negotiator, said Arafat had invited representatives from the United States, Russia, the European Union, Egypt, Jordan, Japan and Norway to the meeting.

Western officials said they were concerned by the depth of distrust between Israelis and Palestinians but they echoed the assessment of Israeli security sources that the kind of violence seen during the last crisis in September was not yet on the cards. Sixty-one Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers died in gun battles then.
"Arafat is in full control of the Palestinian areas. If he wants to keep this crisis off the streets he can," said one Israeli security official.
Netanyahu, on a visit to Moscow, defended his settlement plan and criticised "doomsday" talk.

"We have disagreements. We cannot at every stage of this agreement engage in cataclysmic predictions and talk of crisis and violence," Netanyahu told a news conference. Several Netanyahu aides did not travel to Moscow because of the crisis.
